title: Θεῶν ἀγορή
titleEn: The Gods Bargain over Troy — Iliad 4.1–84
about: The gods are sitting in assembly on Olympus, with Hebe pouring nectar, and watching Troy. To needle Hera, Zeus observes that Menelaus has two goddesses on his side, Hera and Athena, who sit apart looking on, while Aphrodite stays beside Paris and has just rescued him. He asks whether the gods should stir up war again or make peace, with Troy left standing and Helen taken home. Hera and Athena mutter; Athena is silent with rage, but Hera cannot contain hers and protests that her labour would be wasted. Zeus asks what Priam’s house has done to her that she wants Troy plundered, and says he will have the same freedom with her cities, though Ilium was the dearest of all to him. Hera offers her three favourites, Argos, Sparta and Mycenae, and in return asks that Athena be sent to make the Trojans break the oaths first. Zeus agrees and Athena darts down like a star sent as a portent between the armies, leaving the onlookers wondering whether it means war or peace.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ θεοὶ πὰρ Ζηνὶ καθήμενοι ἠγορόωντο
χρυσέῳ ἐν δαπέδῳ, μετὰ δέ σφισι πότνια Ἥβη
νέκταρ ἐοινοχόει·
sentences.i: Now the gods sat beside Zeus in assembly on a golden floor, and among them lady Hebe poured out nectar as their wine;
sentences.n: The scene moves from the plain before Troy to Olympus: οἳ δὲ θεοί is ‘and the gods’, with the old demonstrative οἵ standing almost as an article. πὰρ Ζηνί is παρά ‘beside’ with Ζηνί, an epic dative of Ζεύς that stands beside the commoner Διί (as at 23). καθήμενοι ‘seated’ and ἠγορόωντο ‘were in assembly’ (the imperfect of ἀγοράομαι, in Homer’s uncontracted form) tell us the gods are meeting. Ἥβη is the cupbearer: ἐοινοχόει is the imperfect of οἰνοχοέω ‘pour wine’, and what she pours is νέκταρ ‘nectar’, the gods’ drink. πότνια is ‘lady’.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δὲ χρυσέοις δεπάεσσι
δειδέχατ’ ἀλλήλους, Τρώων πόλιν εἰσορόωντες·
sentences.l:
and they, with golden cups,
were pledging one another, the city of the Trojans looking at;
sentences.i: and with golden cups they pledged one another, looking at the city of the Trojans;
sentences.n: τοί is the old pronoun ‘they’, the gods, and χρυσέοις δεπάεσσι is ‘with golden cups’, the dative plural of δέπας ‘cup’ in the epic ending -εσσι. δειδέχατ’ is δειδέχατο, a past form of the verb ‘greet, welcome’, which with a cup means ‘pledge’; the ending -ατο is the old third plural. Τρώων πόλιν εἰσορόωντες is ‘looking at the city of the Trojans’, a participle in its uncontracted form: the gods watch Troy as they drink. The unit begins in mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκ’ ἐπειρᾶτο Κρονίδης ἐρεθιζέμεν Ἥρην
κερτομίοις ἐπέεσσι παραβλήδην ἀγορεύων·
sentences.l:
At once the son of Cronus tried to provoke Hera
with taunting words, speaking sidelong:
sentences.i: At once the son of Cronus set about provoking Hera, speaking to her with taunting words in a sidelong way:
sentences.n: A speech introduction. ἐπειρᾶτο ‘he tried’ takes the infinitive ἐρεθιζέμεν ‘to provoke’ (the epic ending -έμεν for -ειν), and Κρονίδης ‘son of Cronus’ is Zeus. κερτομίοις ἐπέεσσι is ‘with taunting words’, a dative of means. παραβλήδην is an adverb from παραβάλλω ‘throw beside’; ‘sidelong, slantwise’ is the likely sense, meaning that Zeus does not attack Hera head-on, but the exact force is not certain. ἀγορεύων ‘speaking’ is a participle.

sentences.t:
δοιαὶ μὲν Μενελάῳ ἀρηγόνες εἰσὶ θεάων
Ἥρη τ’ Ἀργείη καὶ Ἀλαλκομενηῒς Ἀθήνη.
sentences.l:
“Two indeed of the goddesses are helpers to Menelaus,
Argive Hera and Alalcomenean Athena.
sentences.i: “Two of the goddesses are helpers to Menelaus: Argive Hera and Alalcomenean Athena.
sentences.n: Zeus begins his taunt. δοιαί ‘two’ is the epic feminine plural of the word for ‘two’, and θεάων is the epic genitive plural of θεά, so ‘two of the goddesses’. ἀρηγόνες ‘helpers’ is the plural of ἀρήγων (from ἀρήγω ‘help’), and Μενελάῳ is the dative of Μενέλαος. Ἀργείη ‘Argive’ is the epithet of Hera that Helen also carries, and Ἀλαλκομενηῒς ‘Alalcomenean’ names Athena by the town of Alalcomenae in Boeotia. μέν looks ahead to the ἀλλά ‘but’ of the next line.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι ταὶ νόσφι καθήμεναι εἰσορόωσαι
τέρπεσθον·
sentences.l:
But indeed those two, sitting apart, looking on,
take their pleasure;
sentences.i: But those two sit apart, looking on, and take their pleasure;
sentences.n: ταί is the feminine plural of the article used as a pronoun, ‘those’, and the two are Hera and Athena of the line before. νόσφι is ‘apart, aside’; καθήμεναι ‘sitting’ and εἰσορόωσαι ‘looking on’ are feminine participles; and τέρπεσθον ‘they take their pleasure’ is a dual (‘the pair of them’), the verb of τέρπομαι ‘enjoy oneself’. Zeus is mocking: the two sit and enjoy the sight, while another goddess does the work. ἤτοι ‘indeed’ is a particle. The unit stops mid-line at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ αὖτε φιλομειδὴς Ἀφροδίτη
αἰεὶ παρμέμβλωκε καὶ αὐτοῦ κῆρας ἀμύνει·
sentences.l:
but beside him, in turn, smile-loving Aphrodite
always keeps close, and his death-fates wards off;
sentences.i: but as for him, smile-loving Aphrodite is always at his side and keeps his fates of death away;
sentences.n: τῷ is a dative, ‘beside him’ with the παρ- of παρμέμβλωκε, and ‘him’ is Paris, whom Zeus does not name: δέ and αὖτε ‘in turn’ set him against Menelaus, whose helpers have just been named. φιλομειδής ‘smile-loving’ is Aphrodite’s stock epithet, translated the same way every time (this edition prints it with one μ). παρμέμβλωκε is the perfect of παραβλώσκω ‘go beside’, so ‘has come and stays beside’; κῆρας ἀμύνει is ‘wards off the death-fates’, where κήρ ‘death-fate’ is a different word from κῆρ ‘heart’, and αὐτοῦ is ‘his’. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: in the fourth foot the short λο of φιλομειδής has to count long (the double μ of φιλομμειδής would make it so), and the φρ of Ἀφροδίτη must not lengthen the vowel before it.

sentences.t: καὶ νῦν ἐξεσάωσεν ὀϊόμενον θανέεσθαι.
sentences.l: and even now she has saved him, thinking he would die.
sentences.i: and now she has saved him, when he thought he was going to die.
sentences.n: ἐξεσάωσεν is the aorist of ἐκσαόω ‘save, rescue’, and καὶ νῦν is ‘even now’: Zeus means Aphrodite’s rescue of Paris in the last part (3.380–382). ὀϊόμενον ‘thinking, expecting’ is a participle of ὀΐομαι, accusative because it agrees with the ‘him’ who was saved, and θανέεσθαι is the epic future infinitive, ‘that he would die’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι νίκη μὲν ἀρηϊφίλου Μενελάου·
sentences.l: But indeed the victory is that of Ares-loved Menelaus;
sentences.i: But the victory, in truth, belongs to Menelaus, dear to Ares;
sentences.n: There is no verb: ‘is’ is understood, and νίκη ‘victory’ is the subject. ἀρηϊφίλου Μενελάου is a genitive of possession, ‘of Menelaus’, with his stock epithet ‘Ares-loved’ (ἀρηΐφιλος, where φίλος means ‘dear to’). Zeus is speaking of the duel of book 3, which Menelaus was winning. μέν is answered by the δέ of the next line, ‘but we…’.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δὲ φραζώμεθ’ ὅπως ἔσται τάδε ἔργα,
ἤ ῥ’ αὖτις πόλεμόν τε κακὸν καὶ φύλοπιν αἰνὴν
ὄρσομεν, ἦ φιλότητα μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισι βάλωμεν.
sentences.l:
but let us ourselves consider how these deeds shall be,
whether again evil war and fearsome battle-din
we shall rouse, or friendship among both sides we shall put.
sentences.i: but let us consider how these things are to turn out: whether we shall stir up evil war and the fearsome din of battle once more, or put friendship between the two sides.
sentences.n: ἡμεῖς ‘we ourselves’ and φραζώμεθ’ ‘let us consider’ (a hortative subjunctive of φράζομαι) bring in the plan, and ὅπως ἔσται τάδε ἔργα is ‘how these deeds shall be’. ἤ ῥ’ … ἦ … is ‘whether … or’, the two choices. ὄρσομεν (from ὄρνυμι ‘rouse, stir up’) and βάλωμεν (aorist subjunctive of βάλλω, here ‘put, set’) are the verbs of the two; φύλοπις αἰνή ‘fearsome battle-din’ is the noise and press of fighting, and μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισι ‘among both sides’. These two lines have a close variant in the Odyssey.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ αὖ πως τόδε πᾶσι φίλον καὶ ἡδὺ γένοιτο,
ἤτοι μὲν οἰκέοιτο πόλις Πριάμοιο ἄνακτος,
αὖτις δ’ Ἀργείην Ἑλένην Μενέλαος ἄγοιτο.
sentences.l:
And if somehow this should become dear and pleasing to all,
then indeed may the city of lord Priam be inhabited,
and Argive Helen again may Menelaus lead home.”
sentences.i: But if somehow this should prove dear and pleasing to everyone, then let the city of lord Priam go on being lived in, and let Menelaus take Argive Helen home again.”
sentences.n: Zeus puts the second choice as a wish. εἰ … γένοιτο ‘if it should come about’ is an optative, and the two optatives οἰκέοιτο ‘may it be inhabited’ and ἄγοιτο ‘may he lead home’ are wishes: may the city stay peopled and may Menelaus take Helen back. τόδε ‘this’ is the plan of peace, πᾶσι ‘to all’, and φίλον καὶ ἡδύ ‘dear and pleasing’. ἄνακτος is the genitive of ἄναξ ‘lord’, and Ἀργείην ‘Argive’ is Helen’s epithet; αὖτις ‘again’ means that she goes back to him. The speech ends.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, αἳ δ’ ἐπέμυξαν Ἀθηναίη τε καὶ Ἥρη·
πλησίαι αἵ γ’ ἥσθην, κακὰ δὲ Τρώεσσι μεδέσθην.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they muttered, Athena and Hera;
close together those two sat, and evils for the Trojans they were contriving.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Athena and Hera muttered; they sat close together, contriving evils for the Trojans.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so he spoke’ (ἔφαθ’ = ἔφατο), closing Zeus’s speech, and αἳ δ’ ‘and they’ turns to the two goddesses. ἐπέμυξαν is an aorist of ἐπιμύζω ‘mutter, murmur’, a low sound made with closed lips. πλησίαι ‘near’ is feminine plural; ἥσθην is the dual of ἧμαι ‘sit’, and μεδέσθην the dual of μέδομαι ‘be minded of, plan’, with κακά ‘evils’ as its object, so ‘the two were contriving evils’. The duals point back to the pair, Hera and Athena; αἵ γ’ is the pronoun ‘those’ with γε.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι Ἀθηναίη ἀκέων ἦν οὐδέ τι εἶπε
σκυζομένη Διὶ πατρί, χόλος δέ μιν ἄγριος ᾕρει·
sentences.l:
Athena indeed was in silence and said nothing at all,
being sullen at father Zeus, and savage anger had hold of her;
sentences.i: Athena for her part stayed silent and said nothing at all, sullen toward her father Zeus, and savage anger took hold of her;
sentences.n: ἤτοι ‘indeed’ sets Athena against Hera in the next line. ἀκέων ἦν ‘was in silence’ and οὐδέ τι εἶπε ‘and said nothing at all’ make the same point twice. σκυζομένη is a participle of σκύζομαι ‘be angry, sulk’, with Διὶ πατρί ‘at father Zeus’. χόλος ‘anger’ is the subject of ᾕρει, the imperfect of αἱρέω ‘seize, take’ with its augment, and μιν is ‘her’; ἄγριος is ‘savage’.

sentences.t: Ἥρῃ δ’ οὐκ ἔχαδε στῆθος χόλον, ἀλλὰ προσηύδα·
sentences.l: But Hera’s breast did not hold the anger, but she spoke out:
sentences.i: But Hera’s breast could not hold her anger, and she spoke out:
sentences.n: Ἥρῃ is a dative of possession, ‘Hera’s’, and στῆθος ‘breast’ is the subject of ἔχαδε, the aorist of χανδάνω ‘hold, contain’. The ἀλλά ‘but’ sets her against Athena’s silence: where Athena keeps the anger in, Hera cannot. προσηύδα ‘she spoke’ is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’, with no object stated; the speech that follows is addressed to Zeus. χόλον ‘anger’ is the same word as in the line before.

sentences.t: αἰνότατε Κρονίδη ποῖον τὸν μῦθον ἔειπες·
sentences.l: “Most dread son of Cronus, what sort of word is this you have spoken?
sentences.i: “Most dreadful son of Cronus, what kind of word is this that you have spoken?
sentences.n: Hera’s first words are a rebuke. αἰνότατε is the vocative of αἰνότατος, the superlative of αἰνός ‘dread’, and Κρονίδη is ‘son of Cronus’, addressed to Zeus. ποῖον τὸν μῦθον ‘what sort of word’ carries the article, which gives the sense ‘this word’, and ἔειπες is the aorist of εἶπον ‘say’ in its epic form with doubled ε.

sentences.t:
πῶς ἐθέλεις ἅλιον θεῖναι πόνον ἠδ’ ἀτέλεστον,
ἱδρῶ θ’ ὃν ἵδρωσα μόγῳ, καμέτην δέ μοι ἵπποι
λαὸν ἀγειρούσῃ, Πριάμῳ κακὰ τοῖό τε παισίν.
sentences.l:
How do you wish to make my toil vain and unaccomplished,
the sweat which I sweated in labour, and my horses grew weary
as I gathered the people, evils for Priam and his sons?
sentences.i: How can you want to make my toil vain and unaccomplished — the sweat I sweated in my labour, with my two horses worn out as I gathered the people to bring evils on Priam and his sons?
sentences.n: One question runs to the end of 28. θεῖναι ‘to make’ has πόνον ‘toil’ as its object and ἅλιον … ἠδ’ ἀτέλεστον ‘vain and unaccomplished’ as what the toil is to be made. ἱδρῶ … ὃν ἵδρωσα is ‘the sweat which I sweated’: the noun and the verb are the same word, and μόγῳ is ‘with labour’. καμέτην is a dual (‘the pair of them grew weary’), which is why ἵπποι ‘horses’ means her two horses. λαὸν ἀγειρούσῃ ‘as I gathered the people’ is a dative participle agreeing with μοι ‘for me’, and Πριάμῳ κακὰ τοῖό τε παισίν ‘evils for Priam and his sons’ says what she gathered them for (τοῖο is the epic genitive ‘his’).

sentences.t: ἕρδ’· ἀτὰρ οὔ τοι πάντες ἐπαινέομεν θεοὶ ἄλλοι.
sentences.l: Do it; but we do not all approve, the other gods.”
sentences.i: Do it; but we other gods do not all approve.”
sentences.n: ἕρδ’ is ἕρδε, the imperative of ἕρδω ‘do’, and ἀτάρ is ‘but’. The negative οὔ goes with πάντες, ‘not all’, so Hera is warning that the gods will not be of one mind. ἐπαινέομεν is ‘we approve’ (ἐπαινέω), and θεοὶ ἄλλοι ‘the other gods’ stands beside ‘we’ in apposition. τοι is a particle, though it can also be read as ‘to you’. The speech ends.

sentences.t: τὴν δὲ μέγ’ ὀχθήσας προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.l: Her, greatly vexed, addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: Greatly troubled, Zeus who gathers the clouds said to her:
sentences.n: A speech introduction. ὀχθήσας is the aorist participle of ὀχθέω ‘be vexed, be troubled’, with μέγα ‘greatly’: Zeus is irritated by Hera’s protest. The rest is the stock introduction: τὴν ‘her’, προσέφη ‘addressed’, and νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς ‘cloud-gatherer Zeus’, translated the same way every time.

sentences.l:
“Strange woman, what so many evils are Priam and Priam’s sons
doing to you, that unceasingly you are eager
to plunder utterly the well-built citadel of Ilium?
sentences.i: “Strange woman, what are Priam and Priam’s sons doing to you, so many evils, that you are eager, without pause, to plunder the well-built citadel of Ilium?
sentences.n: δαιμονίη is the vocative ‘strange woman’, the tone of an exasperated husband. τί νύ σε … τόσσα κακὰ ῥέζουσιν is ‘what are they doing to you, so many evils’: ῥέζουσιν is the present of ῥέζω ‘do’, with Πρίαμος Πριάμοιό τε παῖδες as its subject. ὅ τ’ (ὅ τε) ‘that’ brings in the result, ἀσπερχές is ‘without pause’, and μενεαίνεις ‘you are eager’ governs the infinitive ἐξαλαπάξαι ‘to plunder utterly’. ἐϋκτίμενον πτολίεθρον ‘the well-built citadel’ is the stock phrase for a town, and Ἰλίου is the genitive of Ἴλιος.

sentences.t:
εἰ δὲ σύ γ’ εἰσελθοῦσα πύλας καὶ τείχεα μακρὰ
ὠμὸν βεβρώθοις Πρίαμον Πριάμοιό τε παῖδας
ἄλλους τε Τρῶας, τότε κεν χόλον ἐξακέσαιο.
sentences.l:
But if you yourself, going in at the gates and the long walls,
were to eat raw Priam and Priam’s sons
and the other Trojans, then you might heal your anger.
sentences.i: But if you yourself could go in at the gates and the long walls and eat Priam and Priam’s sons and the other Trojans raw, then you might cure your anger.
sentences.n: A far-fetched supposition, built on optatives. εἰ … βεβρώθοις is ‘if you were to eat’ (βεβρώθοις is an optative of βιβρώσκω ‘eat, devour’), and τότε κεν … ἐξακέσαιο ‘then you might heal’ is the answering optative with κεν. εἰσελθοῦσα ‘going in’ takes πύλας ‘gates’ and τείχεα μακρά ‘long walls’ as the places entered. ὠμόν ‘raw’ is the grimmest word of the passage. ἐξακέσαιο is from ἐξακέομαι ‘heal, cure’, and χόλον is ‘anger’: only eating the Trojans, Zeus says, would cure hers.

sentences.t: ἕρξον ὅπως ἐθέλεις·
sentences.l: Do as you wish;
sentences.i: Do as you wish;
sentences.n: ἕρξον is the aorist imperative of ἕρδω ‘do’, the same verb as ἕρδ’ in Hera’s last line, and ὅπως ἐθέλεις is ‘as you wish’. Zeus gives way in one breath; his condition comes next. The unit stops mid-line at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
μὴ τοῦτό γε νεῖκος ὀπίσσω
σοὶ καὶ ἐμοὶ μέγ’ ἔρισμα μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισι γένηται.
sentences.l:
let not this quarrel, at least, hereafter
for you and for me a great cause of strife among both of us become.
sentences.i: only, let this quarrel not become a great cause of strife between you and me hereafter.
sentences.n: μή with the aorist subjunctive γένηται is a prohibition in the third person, ‘let it not become’. τοῦτό γε νεῖκος ‘this quarrel, at least’ is the subject, ὀπίσσω is ‘hereafter’, and μέγ’ ἔρισμα ‘a great cause of strife’ is the predicate: ἔρισμα, from ἐρίζω ‘quarrel’, is the thing that provokes strife. μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισι ‘among both of us’ is the same phrase as at 16, now about the two of them. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δ’ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσιν·
sentences.l: And another thing to you I will say, and you in your own mind lay it:
sentences.i: And I will tell you something else; lay it up in your own mind:
sentences.n: ἄλλο … ἐρέω is ‘I will tell something else’, where ἐρέω is the epic future of εἶπον, and τοι is ‘to you’. βάλλεο is a middle imperative of βάλλω, ‘put for yourself’ (the ending -εο is for -ου), σῇσιν is the epic dative plural of σός ‘your own’, and ἐνὶ φρεσί is ‘in your mind’. The line is one that the Odyssey also has, and what Zeus is about to say is a warning to remember.

sentences.t:
ὁππότε κεν καὶ ἐγὼ μεμαὼς πόλιν ἐξαλαπάξαι
τὴν ἐθέλω ὅθι τοι φίλοι ἀνέρες ἐγγεγάασι,
μή τι διατρίβειν τὸν ἐμὸν χόλον, ἀλλά μ’ ἐᾶσαι·
sentences.i: Whenever I too am eager to plunder a city — the one I wish for, where men dear to you have their homes — do not hold up my anger, but let me;
sentences.n: Zeus now says what he will ask in return. ὁππότε κεν ‘whenever’ opens the clause, μεμαώς ‘eager’ is a participle, ἐξαλαπάξαι ‘to plunder utterly’ an infinitive, and τὴν points back to πόλιν, the article doing the work of a relative (‘which’) or of ‘that’; either way the sense is ‘the one I wish’, with ‘to plunder’ understood from ἐξαλαπάξαι. ὅθι is ‘where’, τοι is ‘to you’ with φίλοι ‘dear’, and ἐγγεγάασι is the perfect ‘have been born in, live in’. μή τι διατρίβειν is an infinitive standing for a command, ‘do not at all hold up’ (διατρίβω is ‘wear away, delay’), and ἐᾶσαι, the aorist of ἐάω, ‘let me’, is a command too.

sentences.t: καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ σοὶ δῶκα ἑκὼν ἀέκοντί γε θυμῷ·
sentences.l: For I too gave to you, willing, with a spirit unwilling;
sentences.i: For I too gave to you willingly, though with an unwilling spirit;
sentences.n: Zeus says he too has made a concession. δῶκα ‘I gave’ has no object, and the next lines show what it cost him. ἑκών ‘willing’ and ἀέκοντι ‘unwilling’ (agreeing with θυμῷ ‘spirit’) set the act against the spirit behind it, and καὶ γάρ is ‘for indeed’.

sentences.t:
αἳ γὰρ ὑπ’ ἠελίῳ τε καὶ οὐρανῷ ἀστερόεντι
ναιετάουσι πόληες ἐπιχθονίων ἀνθρώπων,
τάων μοι περὶ κῆρι τιέσκετο Ἴλιος ἱρὴ
καὶ Πρίαμος καὶ λαὸς ἐϋμμελίω Πριάμοιο.
sentences.l:
For whatever cities under the sun and the starry heaven
are inhabited, cities of men upon the earth,
of them, beyond all, to me at heart was honoured sacred Ilium
and Priam and the people of Priam of the good ash-spear.
sentences.i: Of all the cities under the sun and the starry heaven that men on earth inhabit, sacred Ilium was honoured by me above them all at heart, and Priam, and the people of Priam of the good ash-spear.
sentences.n: αἳ … πόληες is ‘whichever cities’ (πόληες is the epic plural of πόλις), ναιετάουσι ‘are inhabited’, and ἐπιχθονίων ἀνθρώπων ‘of men on earth’ is a stock phrase. τάων μοι ‘of those, by me’ goes with τιέσκετο, the iterative imperfect of τίω ‘honour’ (‘used to be honoured’); περί is taken with τάων, ‘beyond all of them’ (it could instead be the adverb ‘exceedingly’, as at 53, with the same sense), and κῆρι is the dative of κῆρ ‘heart’. The three subjects, Ἴλιος ἱρή ‘sacred Ilium’ (ἱρή is ἱερή), Πρίαμος and λαός ‘people’, share one singular verb. ἐϋμμελίω Πριάμοιο is ‘of Priam of the good ash-spear’: ἐϋμμελίης is ἐΰ ‘good’ + μελίη ‘ash’, the spear being of ash.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ μοί ποτε βωμὸς ἐδεύετο δαιτὸς ἐΐσης
λοιβῆς τε κνίσης τε· τὸ γὰρ λάχομεν γέρας ἡμεῖς.
sentences.l:
For never did my altar lack the equal feast,
libation and savour; for that is the prize we have received by lot, we ourselves.”
sentences.i: For my altar has never gone short of the equally shared feast, the libation and the savour; that is the prize of honour we gods have received.”
sentences.n: Zeus gives his reason for honouring Ilium: the sacrifices. ἐδεύετο is the imperfect of δεύομαι ‘lack’, which takes the genitive, so δαιτὸς ἐΐσης ‘the equal feast’ (a feast with equal shares), λοιβῆς ‘libation’ and κνίσης ‘savour’ (the smell of burning fat) are the things it never lacked. λάχομεν is the aorist of λαγχάνω ‘obtain by lot’, γέρας ‘prize of honour’ is the gods’ due share, and ἡμεῖς ‘we’ means the gods. The speech ends.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη·
sentences.l: Him then answered ox-eyed lady Hera:
sentences.i: Then ox-eyed lady Hera answered him:
sentences.n: A reply introduction. τὸν ‘him’ is masculine, Zeus, the one answered. βοῶπις ‘ox-eyed’ is Hera’s stock epithet (the usual explanation is large, calm eyes like an ox’s, but the Greek does not say), and πότνια is ‘lady’. ἠμείβετ’ is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ἐμοὶ τρεῖς μὲν πολὺ φίλταταί εἰσι πόληες
Ἄργός τε Σπάρτη τε καὶ εὐρυάγυια Μυκήνη·
sentences.l:
“Indeed, three cities there are by far the dearest to me,
Argos and Sparta and wide-streeted Mycenae;
sentences.i: “Indeed, the three cities dearest to me by far are Argos and Sparta and Mycenae of the wide streets;
sentences.n: ἤτοι ἐμοί ‘indeed, to me’ opens Hera’s answer, and τρεῖς πόληες ‘three cities’ are the subject; φίλταται is the superlative of φίλος ‘dear’, with πολύ ‘by far’. The three are named: Ἄργός (the accent comes from the following τε), Σπάρτη, and Μυκήνη with its epithet εὐρυάγυια ‘wide-streeted’, translated the same way every time. Argos is the city that gives Hera her epithet Ἀργείη at line 8.

sentences.t: τὰς διαπέρσαι ὅτ’ ἄν τοι ἀπέχθωνται περὶ κῆρι·
sentences.l: these sack, whenever they become hateful to you exceedingly at heart;
sentences.i: sack them whenever they grow deeply hateful to you at heart;
sentences.n: τὰς ‘those’ points back to the three cities. διαπέρσαι is an aorist infinitive of διαπέρθω ‘sack utterly’, standing for a command, ‘sack them’. ὅτ’ ἄν … ἀπέχθωνται ‘whenever they become hateful’ is a subjunctive with ἄν, and τοι is ‘to you’; περὶ κῆρι is ‘exceedingly at heart’ (περί an adverb here, κῆρι the dative of κῆρ ‘heart’).

sentences.t: τάων οὔ τοι ἐγὼ πρόσθ’ ἵσταμαι οὐδὲ μεγαίρω.
sentences.l: In front of these I do not stand, nor do I grudge it.
sentences.i: I will not stand in your way over them, nor do I grudge it.
sentences.n: τάων ‘of those (cities)’ is the genitive after πρόσθ’ (πρόσθε) ‘in front of’, and ἵσταμαι is ‘I stand’; to stand in front of a city here means to stand between it and the man who would destroy it, so Hera says she will not defend them. μεγαίρω is ‘I grudge’ (the Odyssey has the same verb), and οὔ … οὐδέ is ‘not … nor’. τοι is a particle.

sentences.t:
εἴ περ γὰρ φθονέω τε καὶ οὐκ εἰῶ διαπέρσαι,
οὐκ ἀνύω φθονέουσ’ ἐπεὶ ἦ πολὺ φέρτερός ἐσσι.
sentences.l:
For even if I begrudge it and do not allow you to sack them,
I accomplish nothing, begrudging, since truly you are much stronger.
sentences.i: For even if I begrudge it and will not let you sack them, I gain nothing by begrudging, since you are far stronger.
sentences.n: εἴ περ ‘even if’ opens a concession. φθονέω τε καὶ οὐκ εἰῶ is ‘I begrudge it and do not allow’ (εἰῶ is ἐῶ ‘allow’), with διαπέρσαι ‘to sack’ as in the line before. οὐκ ἀνύω is ‘I accomplish nothing’ (ἀνύω ‘accomplish’), and φθονέουσ’ ‘begrudging’ is a participle: begrudging gets her nowhere. ἐπεὶ ἦ is ‘since truly’, φέρτερος ‘stronger’ is a comparative with πολύ ‘much’, and ἐσσί is ‘you are’ (the epic form of εἶ).

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ χρὴ καὶ ἐμὸν θέμεναι πόνον οὐκ ἀτέλεστον·
sentences.l: but it is necessary also to make my toil not unaccomplished;
sentences.i: But you must make my toil, too, one that does not go unaccomplished;
sentences.n: ἀλλά marks the turn from giving way to making her own demand. χρή ‘it is necessary’ takes the infinitive θέμεναι ‘to make, put’ (the epic ending -μεναι), and the person who must do it, Zeus, is not named. πόνον οὐκ ἀτέλεστον ‘toil not unaccomplished’ answers ἅλιον πόνον ἠδ’ ἀτέλεστον in 26, which has the same toil and the same ἀτέλεστον.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ θεός εἰμι, γένος δέ μοι ἔνθεν ὅθεν σοί,
καί με πρεσβυτάτην τέκετο Κρόνος ἀγκυλομήτης,
ἀμφότερον γενεῇ τε καὶ οὕνεκα σὴ παράκοιτις
κέκλημαι, σὺ δὲ πᾶσι μετ’ ἀθανάτοισιν ἀνάσσεις.
sentences.l:
For I too am a god, and my race is from where yours is,
and me as eldest begot Cronus of crooked cunning,
both in birth and because your consort
I am called, and you among all the immortals are lord.
sentences.i: For I too am a god, and my family comes from the same stock as yours, and Cronus of crooked cunning begot me as the eldest, both by birth and because I am called your wife, while you rule among all the immortals.
sentences.n: Hera argues from her rank. θεός εἰμι is ‘I am a god’ (the noun is used of a goddess), and γένος δέ μοι ἔνθεν ὅθεν σοί is ‘my family is from where yours is’, ἐστί being understood, since both are children of Cronus. πρεσβυτάτην ‘eldest’ is a superlative and τέκετο is the aorist middle of τίκτω, used here of the father, ‘begot’. ἀμφότερον ‘in both ways’ is followed by two reasons, γενεῇ ‘by birth’ and οὕνεκα ‘because’ (epic for ὅτι); κέκλημαι ‘I am called’ is the perfect passive of καλέω, and παράκοιτις ‘consort’ means a wife. ἀνάσσεις ‘you are lord’ is the verb of ἄναξ, and ἀγκυλομήτης ‘of crooked cunning’ is Cronus’s stock epithet, whose exact sense is uncertain.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι μὲν ταῦθ’ ὑποείξομεν ἀλλήλοισι,
σοὶ μὲν ἐγώ, σὺ δ’ ἐμοί·
sentences.l:
But indeed these things we will yield to each other,
I to you, and you to me;
sentences.i: But we will give way to each other in these things, I to you and you to me;
sentences.n: ὑποείξομεν is the future of ὑπείκω ‘give way, yield’ (in Homer’s ὑπο- form), ἀλλήλοισι is ‘to each other’, and ταῦθ’ is ταῦτα ‘these things’. σοὶ μὲν ἐγώ, σὺ δ’ ἐμοί is a compact ‘I (shall yield) to you, and you to me’: Hera offers a bargain in which each gives way to the other. ἀλλ’ ἤτοι is ‘but indeed’. The unit stops mid-line at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δ’ ἕψονται θεοὶ ἄλλοι
ἀθάνατοι·
sentences.l:
and thereupon will follow the other gods,
the immortals;
sentences.i: and the other gods, the immortals, will follow along;
sentences.n: ἐπί is an adverb, ‘besides, after’, with ἕψονται, the future of ἕπομαι ‘follow’. θεοὶ ἄλλοι ἀθάνατοι is ‘the other gods, the immortals’: ἀθάνατοι is in apposition and stands at the start of line 64, so the sentence runs over the line-end. The other gods will fall in with whatever Zeus and Hera agree. The unit begins and ends mid-line, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
σὺ δὲ θᾶσσον Ἀθηναίῃ ἐπιτεῖλαι
ἐλθεῖν ἐς Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν φύλοπιν αἰνήν,
sentences.l:
and you, quickly, to Athena give charge
to go into the fearsome battle-din of Trojans and Achaeans,
sentences.i: and you, quickly, give Athena the charge to go into the fearsome din of battle of the Trojans and the Achaeans,
sentences.n: σύ ‘you’ is Zeus, and ἐπιτεῖλαι is an aorist infinitive of ἐπιτέλλω ‘charge, give orders’, used as a command; the person charged is in the dative, Ἀθηναίῃ, and ἐλθεῖν ‘to go’ says the task. θᾶσσον is the comparative of ταχύς ‘quick’, used here for urgency, ‘at once’. ἐς Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν φύλοπιν αἰνήν is ‘into the fearsome battle-din of Trojans and Achaeans’; φύλοπις is the noise of battle, as at 15. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
πειρᾶν δ’ ὥς κε Τρῶες ὑπερκύδαντας Ἀχαιοὺς
ἄρξωσι πρότεροι ὑπὲρ ὅρκια δηλήσασθαι.
sentences.l:
and to try how the Trojans might first begin
to do harm to the exulting Achaeans, beyond the oaths.”
sentences.i: and to try to make the Trojans the first to start doing harm to the exulting Achaeans, in breach of the oaths.”
sentences.n: πειρᾶν ‘to try’ is a second infinitive after ἐπιτεῖλαι, so Athena is charged both to go and to try. ὥς κε … ἄρξωσι is ‘how they might begin’, an aorist subjunctive with κε, with πρότεροι ‘first’, and δηλήσασθαι ‘to do harm’ is an aorist infinitive of δηλέομαι. ὑπερκύδαντας ‘exulting’ is from ὑπέρ + κῦδος ‘glory’; its exact sense is not certain, and ‘exulting, overweening in their glory’ is the usual guess. ὑπὲρ ὅρκια ‘beyond the oaths’ means in breach of the oaths sworn in book 3. The speech ends.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and did not disobey, the father of men and of gods;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and the father of men and of gods did not disobey her;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so she spoke’ closes Hera’s speech, and οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε ‘and did not disobey’ is the aorist of ἀπιθέω, the opposite of πείθομαι ‘obey’. The subject is held to the end of the line: πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε ‘the father of men and of gods’ is Zeus.

sentences.t: αὐτίκ’ Ἀθηναίην ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l: At once to Athena winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: At once he spoke winged words to Athena:
sentences.n: A speech introduction. αὐτίκ’ is ‘at once’, and Ἀθηναίην is the object of προσηύδα ‘he spoke to’. ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ is the stock phrase for words that fly from speaker to hearer, translated the same way every time.

sentences.t: αἶψα μάλ’ ἐς στρατὸν ἐλθὲ μετὰ Τρῶας καὶ Ἀχαιούς,
sentences.l: “Very quickly to the army go, among the Trojans and the Achaeans,
sentences.i: “Go very quickly to the army, among the Trojans and the Achaeans,
sentences.n: αἶψα μάλ’ is ‘very quickly’, and ἐλθέ is an aorist imperative of ἔρχομαι. στρατόν is ‘army’, and μετὰ Τρῶας καὶ Ἀχαιούς is ‘among the Trojans and the Achaeans’, with μετά and the accusative meaning ‘into the midst of’. The sentence continues in the next two lines, which repeat 66–67 word for word.

sentences.t:
πειρᾶν δ’ ὥς κε Τρῶες ὑπερκύδαντας Ἀχαιοὺς
ἄρξωσι πρότεροι ὑπὲρ ὅρκια δηλήσασθαι.
sentences.l:
and to try how the Trojans might first begin
to do harm to the exulting Achaeans, beyond the oaths.”
sentences.i: and to try to make the Trojans the first to start doing harm to the exulting Achaeans, in breach of the oaths.”
sentences.n: These two lines are 66–67 word for word: Zeus gives Athena the very charge that Hera named. πειρᾶν ‘to try’ depends on the command ἐλθέ ‘go’ of the line before, and the rest is as at 66–67, with ὑπερκύδαντας ‘exulting’ of uncertain sense. The speech ends.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ὄτρυνε πάρος μεμαυῖαν Ἀθήνην,
βῆ δὲ κατ’ Οὐλύμποιο καρήνων ἀΐξασα.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, he urged on Athena, already eager,
and she went down from the peaks of Olympus, darting;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and urged on Athena, who was already eager; and she went darting down from the peaks of Olympus;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών is ‘so having spoken’; ὄτρυνε is an unaugmented past of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, and πάρος μεμαυῖαν ‘already eager’ says that Athena needs no urging. βῆ δὲ κατ’ Οὐλύμποιο καρήνων ἀΐξασα is a line the poet has already used for Athena’s descent from Olympus: κατά ‘down from’ takes the genitive, καρήνων ‘peaks’ is the epic plural of κάρηνον, and ἀΐξασα ‘darting’ is an aorist participle of ἀΐσσω.

sentences.t:
οἷον δ’ ἀστέρα ἧκε Κρόνου πάϊς ἀγκυλομήτεω
ἢ ναύτῃσι τέρας ἠὲ στρατῷ εὐρέϊ λαῶν
λαμπρόν·
sentences.i: Like a star that the son of Cronus of crooked cunning sent as a portent, either to sailors or to a wide army of people, a bright one;
sentences.n: A simile begins, and it closes at 78 with τῷ ἐϊκυῖ’ ‘like that’. οἷον ‘like’ introduces the star, ἀστέρα, which the son of Cronus (Κρόνου πάϊς ἀγκυλομήτεω, ‘of crooked cunning’) sent; ἧκε is the aorist ‘sent’, in a simile’s timeless sense. τέρας ‘portent’ is in apposition to the star, with ναύτῃσι ‘to sailors’, ἢ … ἠέ ‘either … or’ and στρατῷ εὐρέϊ λαῶν ‘to a wide army of people’. λαμπρόν ‘bright’ agrees with ἀστέρα. The unit stops mid-line at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: τοῦ δέ τε πολλοὶ ἀπὸ σπινθῆρες ἵενται·
sentences.l: and from it many sparks fly off;
sentences.i: and from it many sparks fly off;
sentences.n: τοῦ ‘from it’, the star, is a genitive of source. ἀπὸ … ἵενται is ‘fly off’, a preposition separated from its verb (tmesis, for ἀφίενται), with ἵενται the middle or passive of ἵημι. σπινθῆρες ‘sparks’ is the subject, with πολλοί ‘many’, and δέ τε is ‘and’ with the epic τε of general statements. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t: τῷ ἐϊκυῖ’ ἤϊξεν ἐπὶ χθόνα Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη,
sentences.l: Like that, she darted upon the earth, Pallas Athena,
sentences.i: Like that star, Pallas Athena darted down to the earth,
sentences.n: τῷ ἐϊκυῖ’ ‘like it’ closes the simile: ἐϊκυῖα is the feminine perfect participle of ἔοικα ‘be like’, with the dative τῷ ‘to it’, the star, and it agrees with Athena. ἤϊξεν is the aorist of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’, the verb of ἀΐξασα in 74. ἐπὶ χθόνα is ‘onto the ground’, and Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη ‘Pallas Athena’ fills the end of the line.

sentences.t: κὰδ δ’ ἔθορ’ ἐς μέσσον·
sentences.l: and she leapt down into the midst;
sentences.i: and she leapt down into the midst;
sentences.n: κὰδ is κατά with its last letter taken over by the next consonant, and it is separated from its verb: κὰδ … ἔθορ’ is ‘leapt down’ (ἔθορε, aorist of θρῴσκω ‘leap’). ἐς μέσσον is ‘into the middle’, and the Greek does not say of what; the next line shows the Trojans and Achaeans looking on. The unit stops mid-line at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
θάμβος δ’ ἔχεν εἰσορόωντας
Τρῶάς θ’ ἱπποδάμους καὶ ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.l:
and wonder held those looking on,
the horse-taming Trojans and the well-greaved Achaeans.
sentences.i: and wonder held them as they looked on, the Trojans, tamers of horses, and the well-greaved Achaeans.
sentences.n: θάμβος ‘wonder’ is the subject of ἔχεν ‘held’, an unaugmented past, and εἰσορόωντας ‘those looking on’ is the object, a participle in its uncontracted form. Τρῶάς … καὶ … Ἀχαιούς, ‘the Trojans and the Achaeans’, stands beside it to say who they are. ἱπποδάμους ‘horse-taming’ and ἐϋκνήμιδας ‘well-greaved’ are stock epithets, translated the same way every time. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t: ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκεν ἰδὼν ἐς πλησίον ἄλλον·
sentences.l: And thus someone would say, looking to another close by:
sentences.i: And as each looked at the one beside him, he would say something like this:
sentences.n: ὧδε is ‘thus’, and τις ‘someone’ is any one of the onlookers. εἴπεσκεν is an iterative imperfect of εἶπον, ‘used to say, would say’ (the -σκ- marks repetition), so each man says something like what follows. ἰδών ‘looking’ is a participle, and ἐς πλησίον ἄλλον is ‘to another close by’.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥ’ αὖτις πόλεμός τε κακὸς καὶ φύλοπις αἰνὴ
ἔσσεται, ἢ φιλότητα μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισι τίθησι
Ζεύς, ὅς τ’ ἀνθρώπων ταμίης πολέμοιο τέτυκται.
sentences.l:
“Truly either again evil war and fearsome battle-din
will be, or friendship among both sides is being set
by Zeus, who of men has been made the steward of war.”
sentences.i: “Either evil war and the fearsome din of battle will come again, or Zeus is setting friendship between the two sides — Zeus, who has been made the steward of war for men.”
sentences.n: The onlookers voice the same two possibilities that Zeus put to the gods at 15–16, though they cannot have heard him: ἦ ῥ’ is ‘truly’ and ἢ is ‘or’, so the sentence is ‘truly either … or’; the edition ends it with a full stop, but ἦ ῥ’ … ἢ could also be read as a question, ‘will there be … or is Zeus setting …?’. ἔσσεται is ‘will be’, φιλότητα μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισι is ‘friendship among both sides’, and τίθησι ‘sets, puts’ has Ζεύς as its subject, held to the start of 84. ὅς τ’ … ταμίης πολέμοιο τέτυκται is ‘who has been made steward of war’: ταμίης ‘steward’ is one who allots, τέτυκται is the perfect passive of τεύχω ‘make’, and ἀνθρώπων ‘of men’ goes with ταμίης. The speech ends.
